title: The butter thief
hookLine: a toddler with butter on his chin, a line of happy monkeys, and the neighbors at his mother's door
last: A THREAD CAN HOLD A PROMISE.

cards: A village of cowherds on the banks of the Yamuna, early morning. The women have been churning since before dawn, and the fresh butter is hung high in clay pots, out of reach. It doesn't help.
By noon a pot is cracked, the butter is gone, and a line of monkeys is licking their fingers. The culprit is about three years old. He has butter on his chin, and he swears he was asleep.
The women march to his mother's door to complain, and halfway through complaining, they start laughing.

teach.h: A THIEF THE WHOLE VILLAGE LOVES.
teach.b: The boy is Krishna, the same Krishna you left holding Arjuna's reins on day seventy-seven. The Bhagavata Purana gives the neighbors' complaint as a list. He lets the calves loose before milking time.
He steals the curd and the butter. He feeds it to the monkeys, and if the monkeys won't eat, he breaks the pot. When the pots are hung out of reach, he stacks up stools and a mortar and climbs.
And when he's caught, he looks so innocent that nobody can stay angry. That's why the nickname stuck. In Hindi he's Makhan Chor, the butter thief, and it's always said with love.

teach.h: THE SAME KRISHNA, HONORED AS GOD.
teach.b: This same Krishna is honored as God. In the Gita he speaks as the source of everything, and in the same life he's a toddler being scolded by his mother. Devotees don't treat that as a contradiction.
Many say it's the point: God close enough to be fed, chased, scolded and loved like a child.
So Krishna comes with many faces.

teach.h: THE BABY ON THE HOME SHRINE.
teach.b: The baby born in a prison at midnight. The butter thief. The cowherd boy whose flute pulls the whole village outside.
The friend driving a chariot onto a battlefield. Many people love one face most. In many homes there's a small brass baby Krishna, crawling, a sweet in one hand, often called Laddu Gopal.
Families bathe him, dress him and offer him food each day, the way you'd care for a little child. Gopala means a cowherd, the one who looks after the cows. And the butter?
Some devotees say it stands for a soft, well-churned heart, and that a heart is what he really comes to steal.

how: Many Hindu homes keep a small image of baby Krishna, often called Laddu Gopal, and bathe, dress and offer food to him each day; the butter-thief stories are told and sung, especially around Janmashtami.

o: a demon who steals the village's milk
a cowherd who guards the butter pots
the child Krishna, loved for stealing butter

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the butter thief, said with love
a cowherd, who looks after the cows
baby Krishna, cared for at home

s: to devotees, the butter-thief stories make Krishna less divine
many devotees say that's the point: God close enough to be fed, chased and scolded.
in the Bhagavata Purana, the neighbors complain to Krishna's mother
they list the stolen butter, the broken pots and the monkeys, and can't stay angry.
Laddu Gopal is a grown Krishna with a flute
Laddu Gopal is baby Krishna, crawling, with a sweet in his hand.

games.q: you're Yashoda. the neighbors are at your door listing what your toddler stole. he's standing behind you with butter on his chin, swearing he was asleep. what happens?
o: you punish him in front of everyone.
you try to scold him, and everyone ends up laughing.
you pay the neighbors back and say nothing.
games.why: in the Bhagavata, the complaints pile up, but his innocent face wins. nobody can stay angry with him for long.

practice: Picture someone small you love caught mid-mischief, a child, a sibling, a pet: wide eyes, guilty grin, evidence on the chin. Notice the annoyance, maybe, and right under it something softer, and stay with the softer thing.
If you pray, you can hold Krishna's child face in your mind the same way.

wordCard.voice: Makhan Chor. The butter thief: Krishna as a little boy, scolded and adored, and still honored as God. Today's word.

orig.note: Hindi: makhan, butter, and chor, thief. Krishna's best-loved childhood nickname.

carryVoice: Your line: close enough to scold. A God you can chase around the kitchen. Day eighty-five, and the butter's gone.
